label: trig batch — unit circle dials, right-triangle ratios, wave parameters

widget.prompt: Drag the acute angle to 37° and read the opp/hyp card — then resize the whole triangle and watch whether that reading moves.
widget.successFeedback: opp/hyp ≈ 0.6 at 37°, and resizing changed nothing. That is the entire reason sine can be a function of the ANGLE alone: the 3-4-5 triangle and the 6-8-10 triangle are the same shape, so they hand back the same ratio.
widget.lowFeedback: The angle is under 37° — the opposite side is too short relative to the hypotenuse.
widget.highFeedback: The angle is over 37° — the opposite side is too long relative to the hypotenuse.
widget.scaleFeedback: Resize the triangle at least twice before checking. One reading at one size proves nothing about every similar triangle.

widget.prompt: Hypotenuse 20, θ = 30°. Drag to 30° and read opp/hyp, then use it to find the opposite side.
widget.successFeedback: opp/hyp = 0.5 at 30°, so the opposite side is 0.5 × 20 = 10. Solving for a side is always this: the ratio is fixed by the angle, and the hypotenuse scales it.
widget.scaleFeedback: Resize the triangle a couple of times first; the ratio must hold at every size for the method to work.

widget.prompt: sin θ = 0.5. Drag the angle until the opp/hyp card reads 0.5 — that is what an inverse sine does.
widget.successFeedback: θ = 30°. Finding an angle from a ratio is the same table read backwards, which is all sin⁻¹ means: not a new operation, but the question 'which angle gives this ratio?'.
widget.lowFeedback: opp/hyp is still below 0.5 — open the angle further.
widget.highFeedback: opp/hyp has gone past 0.5 — close the angle a little.
widget.scaleFeedback: Resize the triangle before checking; the angle that gives 0.5 must not depend on the triangle's size.

dials.feedback: The swing is wrong. Amplitude is the distance from the midline to the crest, not the crest's height above zero.
The wave is centred on the wrong level. The midline is the horizontal line the wave oscillates about.

widget.prompt: Build y = 2 sin x + 1 with the dials, then read off its maximum.
widget.successFeedback: Maximum 3 — midline 1 plus amplitude 2. Watch which dial did what: amplitude changed the SWING and midline changed the CENTRE, and the maximum is their sum, never just the amplitude.
widget.lowFeedback: The wave is not yet y = 2 sin x + 1.
widget.highFeedback: The wave has overshot y = 2 sin x + 1.

dials.feedback: The wave is not repeating at the right rate. The b in sin(bx) counts how many full cycles fit where one used to.

widget.prompt: Set the dial to build y = sin(2x), then read how far it travels before repeating.
widget.successFeedback: Period π ≈ 3.14 — half of 2π, because b = 2 packs two cycles into the space of one. Period = 2π ÷ b, and the dial makes the division visible rather than remembered.
widget.lowFeedback: The wave is still stretched — fewer cycles than y = sin(2x).
widget.highFeedback: The wave is compressed past y = sin(2x) — too many cycles.

dials.feedback: The wheel's radius is wrong. The amplitude is how far the rider swings above and below the centre.
The wheel is at the wrong height. The midline is the centre of the wheel above the ground.

widget.prompt: Build the Ferris wheel h(t) = 25 − 20 cos t with the dials, then read the rider's lowest point.
widget.successFeedback: Minimum 5 feet — centre 25 minus radius 20. The cosine starts at its own maximum, so the minus sign puts the rider at the BOTTOM at t = 0, which is where a Ferris wheel loads.
widget.lowFeedback: The wheel is not yet 20 feet of swing about a 25-foot centre.
widget.highFeedback: The wheel has passed 20 feet of swing about a 25-foot centre.

dials.feedback: The swing is wrong. Amplitude is half the distance between the high and the low.
The centre is wrong. The midline is the average of the high and the low.

widget.prompt: Daily temperature runs between 30° and 10°. Build the model with the dials.
widget.successFeedback: Amplitude 10, midline 20: half the 20-degree spread, centred on their average. Every wave-fitting problem starts with these two — (high − low)/2 and (high + low)/2 — before any period work begins.
widget.lowFeedback: The wave does not yet run between 10 and 30.
widget.highFeedback: The wave now swings past the 10-to-30 range.

widget.prompt: Drag the point around the unit circle to 30° and read both coordinates, then square them and add.
widget.successFeedback: The coordinates are (cos θ, sin θ), and the point sits on a circle of radius 1 — so cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 at EVERY angle, not just this one. The Pythagorean identity is the circle's equation wearing trigonometric clothes.
widget.lowFeedback: Not at 30° yet — keep dragging round.

widget.prompt: One acute angle is 37°. Drag to it, read adj/hyp, and note what the other acute angle must be.
widget.successFeedback: The other acute angle is 53°, because the two must total 90°. Solving a right triangle completely means one angle plus one side is enough — the third angle comes free, and the ratios supply the rest.
widget.scaleFeedback: Resize the triangle a couple of times; the ratio at 37° must not depend on how big it is.

widget.prompt: A drone hovers 120 m up; the angle of depression to the pad is 27°. Drag to 27° and read opp/adj — the ratio that links the height to the ground distance.
widget.successFeedback: tan 27° ≈ 0.51, so the ground distance is 120 ÷ 0.51 ≈ 235 m. Depression from the drone equals elevation from the pad — alternate angles across parallel horizontals — which is why one angle serves both viewpoints.
widget.lowFeedback: Under 27° — opp/adj is reading too small.
widget.highFeedback: Over 27° — opp/adj is reading too large.
widget.scaleFeedback: Resize the triangle before checking; the tangent of 27° is fixed by the angle alone.

widget.prompt: Build y = −2(x − 1)² + 8 with the three dials, then read its maximum.
widget.successFeedback: Maximum 8, at the vertex (1, 8). The negative a is what makes it a maximum rather than a minimum — flip a positive and the vertex changes from the lowest point to the highest without moving at all.
widget.shapeFeedback: The opening is wrong. A negative a opens downward; its size controls how narrow the curve is.
widget.vertexFeedback: The vertex is not at (1, 8) yet — h shifts it sideways, k shifts it up.

widget.prompt: Build y = x² + 3 and read the smallest output the curve ever produces.
widget.successFeedback: Minimum 3 — the vertex. The range is everything from 3 upward, because a squared term is never negative and the +3 lifts the whole curve. Range is read off the vertex, not the equation.
widget.shapeFeedback: Leave a at 1 — this parent curve is not stretched.
widget.vertexFeedback: The vertex is not at (0, 3) yet.

widget.prompt: Build y = x² + 2x − 3 in vertex form and count how many times it meets the x-axis.
widget.successFeedback: Vertex (−1, −4), and the curve crosses twice. Degree caps the zeros — a degree-2 curve can meet the axis at most twice, a degree-5 at most five times — and the vertex's position decides how many of those actually happen.
widget.shapeFeedback: Leave a at 1; the leading coefficient here is 1.
widget.vertexFeedback: Not at the vertex. Half of 2 is 1, so the vertex sits at x = −1.

widget.prompt: Flatten the curve to a = 0 and lift it to k = 5 — the height where a line with y-intercept 5 crosses the vertical axis.
widget.successFeedback: With a = 0 the curve is a horizontal line at 5, which is exactly where y = 2x + 5 meets the y-axis: the y-intercept is the output when x = 0. The x-intercept is the mirror question — the input when the output is 0.
widget.shapeFeedback: Bring a to 0 to flatten the curve out of its parabola shape.
widget.vertexFeedback: The height is not 5 yet — k sets it.

refusals.title: The Radian, Degrees ↔ Radians, Arc Length
refusals.why: Unit conversion and arc length s = rθ. unitCircleExplore drags an ANGLE and traces a wave; its dials are amplitude, midline, angularScale and phase. Nothing in it represents the radius as a variable, so arc length cannot be modelled, and a degree/radian conversion has no manipulable state at all — it is a restatement, not a quantity. circleMeasureExplore's arcSector mode is the closest candidate and belongs to circle geometry, not the trig course's unit work. Refused.

refusals.title: Shadows Wires & Surveys, Choosing the Tool
refusals.why: rt-04-03's step is a two-unknown survey equation x·tan55° = (x+30)·tan40°; triangleSolve holds ONE triangle and cannot represent two triangles sharing a base. rt-05-04 asks which tool fits a given configuration — a classification over methods, the same shape as the statistics checklist refusals. Refused.

refusals.title: The two remaining trig courses
refusals.why: NOT REFUSED — deferred. unitCircleExplore has ghost modes (double | negate | cofunction | sum) that look built for exactly the sum/difference and double-angle identities, and a branch field that may carry inverse-trig restriction. Judging fit needs the ghost semantics read from a donor, which this batch did not have room for. Recording as deferred so the fit rate is not inflated by counting them either way.
